item.title: A $(3/2+\varepsilon)$-Approximation for Weighted 3-Set Packing
item.description: arXiv:2611.28541v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We give a deterministic $(3/2+\varepsilon)$-approximation for weighted $3$-set packing, for every fixed rational $\varepsilon>0$, improving on the 1.6908-approximation reported by Tong and Xu (2026). The algorithm has two phases. It first performs bounded local search using a rounded $12/7$-power potential. It then combines compatible exchanges that insert at most three sets and increase the original weight. The analysis relates the gap left by the first phase to the gain available to the second phase. We prove a structural inequality that bounds the weight of a comparison packing by $3/2$ times the current weight plus one sixth of a sum of small-exchange gains. Each gain accounts for all sets that the exchange must delete. A greedy rule recovers enough of these gains to obtain the approximation guarantee. We derive the structural bound from local optimality by analyzing finite computation trees and averaging the error caused by their limited depth. The running time is $n^{4^{O(1/\varepsilon)}}\operatorname{poly}(L)$, where $n$ is the number of input sets and $L$ is the input encoding length. The same guarantee holds for maximum-weight independent set in induced $K_{1,4}$-free graphs.
item.dc:creator: Changjun Wang, Daorong Yu, Wei Yu

item.title: Odd Chromatic Number of Graph Classes: Bounds and Structural Results
item.description: arXiv:2611.29332v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A proper coloring of a graph $G$ is called an \emph{odd coloring} if, for every non-isolated vertex $v\in V(G)$, there exists a color that occurs an odd number of times in the open neighborhood of $v$. For a graph $G$, the minimum number of colors required for such a coloring is called the {\em odd chromatic number}, denoted by $\chi_{o}(G)$. The odd chromatic number has been well-studied from both combinatorial and algorithmic perspectives, and several bounds on $\chi_o(G)$ are known. In this paper, we establish tight bounds on $\chi_o(G)$ for several graph classes. In particular, we obtain the following results: 1. For every block-cactus graph $G$, we prove that $\chi_o(G) \leq \max \{5,\omega(G)+1\}$, where $\omega(G)$ denotes the clique number of $G$. 2. For block graphs and proper interval graphs, we establish the bounds $\omega(G) \leq \chi_o(G) \leq \omega(G)+1$. 3. For a bipartite circle graph, we prove that $\chi_o(G) \leq 6$. This settles an open question asked by Davis et al., 2026. 4. For every biconvex bipartite graph $G$, we prove that $\chi_o(G) \leq 5$. 5. For $C_4$-free cographs $G$, we establish the bound $\chi_o(G) \leq \omega(G)+1$. Moreover, we characterize block graphs, proper interval graphs, and cactus graphs based on their odd chromatic number.
item.dc:creator: Musarof Hossain, Sandeep Kumar, Vikash Tripathi, Mirza Galib Anwarul Husain Baig

item.title: Via a New LP Relaxation: Stronger Performance Guarantees for WSEPT, and an LP-Based Proof of Kawaguchi & Kyan
item.description: arXiv:2611.30731v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a new linear programming relaxation for minimizing the total weighted completion time on identical parallel machines. Its right-hand side is supermodular, so the relaxation can be solved by a greedy algorithm. We show that the WSPT rule is within a factor $\frac{1}{2}(1 + \sqrt{2})$ of the optimal LP value. This bounds the integrality gap of the relaxation and gives a short, LP-based proof of the tight bound of Kawaguchi and Kyan on the performance of WSPT. We then turn to the stochastic version of the problem, in which processing times are independent random variables whose squared coefficients of variation are at most~$\Delta$. A variance-corrected version of the new LP relaxation is valid for all non-anticipatory policies, and we show that WSEPT is within a factor $1 + (1 + \Delta)/(3 + \sqrt{7 + 2 \Delta})$ of it for $\Delta \ge 1$, for any number of machines. This is $O(\sqrt\Delta)$, whereas all previous guarantees for this problem grow linearly in $\Delta$. Up to a constant factor, our bound matches the known $\Omega(\sqrt\Delta)$ lower bound for WSEPT. For $\Delta \le 1$, we recover the best known bounds.
item.dc:creator: Maximilian von Aspern, Andreas S. Schulz, Eugenio Vairo

item.title: Roman-Type Domination on Bisplit Graphs: Hardness and Inapproximability
item.description: arXiv:2611.30988v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Inspired by the structure and name of split graphs, bisplit graphs have three independent sets $I,A,B$, where every vertex of $A$ is adjacent to every vertex of $B$, and vertices of $I$ may have arbitrary neighborhoods in the core $A\cup B$. Thus they have a complete bipartite core together with the remaining vertices, making them a structured setting in which to study how core size affects complexity. Mann and Fernau's construction already implies NP-completeness of perfect Roman domination on bisplit graphs with a singleton core side \citep[Theorem~20]{mann-fernau-pr}. Motivated by this result, we study all four Roman-type domination problems across further core-size regimes: we prove NP-completeness when one core side has size one or two, and when both sides have size at least three. For perfect Italian domination, even deciding whether prescribed core labels of total weight two can be extended is NP-complete on bipartite bisplit graphs. Approximation is also addressed: for every fixed $0<\varepsilon<1$, unless $\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}$, no $n^{1-\varepsilon}$-approximation exists for perfect Roman domination when one core side has fixed size $1$, $2$, or $3$, or for perfect Italian domination on bipartite bisplit graphs whose two core sides grow with the input. All four problems are fixed-parameter tractable for both parameters. Given supplied modulators of size $k$, the running-time bases, in the order Roman, perfect Roman, Italian, and perfect Italian, are $4,11,11,18$ for cluster vertex deletion and $6,11,11,18$ for biclique-cluster vertex deletion, up to polynomial factors. The $4^k$ Roman cluster-deletion bound is known; the other bounds follow from our dynamic programs. To our knowledge, the latter parameter has not previously been studied explicitly for domination variants.
item.dc:creator: M. S. Manjusha, P. Renjith

item.title: Cliques, Quasi-Cliques, and Bicliques in Random Graphs: Sampling and Algorithms
item.description: arXiv:2611.28307v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study the algorithmic problem of finding dense subgraphs - cliques, quasi-cliques, and bicliques - in Erd\H{o}s-R\'enyi random graphs. While the extremal structure of cliques in $G(n,1/2)$ is well understood, efficiently locating large cliques remains a central algorithmic challenge. We introduce a new perspective on this problem: the classical Grimmett-McDiarmid greedy algorithm implicitly defines a near-uniform sampler over cliques of size $(1-o(1))\log n$. Building on this observation, we develop a sampling-based framework for finding larger cliques. In particular, for every $\eta>0$, we give an algorithm that finds a clique of size $(1+\eta)\log n$ in time $n^{(\eta^2/2+o(1))\log n}$ - the first smooth trade-off between clique size and running time in this regime, improving on the previously best-known running time of $n^{(1/2+o(1))\log n}$. We further show that improved sampling algorithms for cliques of size $(1+\eta)\log n$ translate into faster algorithms for finding a maximum clique. Beyond cliques, we give a deterministic algorithm that enumerates all maximum $\gamma$-quasi-cliques in $G(n,p)$ in time matching their count up to lower-order factors, and extend this to random bipartite graphs $G(n,n,p)$, establishing new concentration bounds for quasi-bicliques together with analogous enumeration algorithms. Finally, we study unbalanced bicliques in $G(n,n,p)$. For each $s \in [n]$, we obtain a concentration bound on the largest $t = t_{\max}(s)$ for which an $(s,t)$-biclique exists, and show that when $s = \omega(\log n)$, a simple greedy algorithm finds an $(s,(1-o(1))t_{\max}(s))$-biclique in linear time with high probability - demonstrating that greedy is near-optimal in this regime.
item.dc:creator: Thanh Le, A. Pavan, Xavier P\'erez-Gim\'enez, N. V. Vinodchandran

item.title: The Gerards-Schrijver conjecture on the Edmonds-Johnson property is false
item.description: arXiv:2611.28580v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: An integral matrix $A$ has the Edmonds-Johnson property if, for all integral vectors $b,c,l,u$, the first Chv\'atal closure of $\{x: b\le Ax\le c,\ l\le x\le u\}$ equals its integer hull. Gerards and Schrijver conjectured that a totally half-modular matrix has the Edmonds-Johnson property if and only if it has no minor equal to one of two specific matrices, of size $3\times3$ and $3\times4$. We disprove this conjecture. We give a totally half-modular $5\times6$ matrix that does not have the Edmonds-Johnson property and has no minor equal to either matrix. It is a minimal obstruction: every proper minor has the Edmonds-Johnson property. The proofs work on a graph whose edges are the rows and bounds of the matrix, and on which the minor operations act by deleting, contracting and halving edges. For minimality, we reduce every proper minor to two classes of matrices known to have the Edmonds-Johnson property.
item.dc:creator: Alberto Del Pia

item.title: Note on polychromatic coloring of hereditary hypergraph families III
item.description: arXiv:2611.28664v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: For every integer $h\ge4$ we construct a hereditary family of hypergraphs with $m_2=h$ and \[ m_3\ge 2(h-1)+2\left\lfloor\frac{h-1}{3}\right\rfloor+1 \approx \frac{8}{3}m_2. \] This improves the lower bound $m_3\ge 2m_2$ from the preceding notes for every $m_2\ge4$. We also show that the worst-case integrality gap of the weighted transversal problem over hereditary families with $m_2\le h$ is between $h-1$ and $5000h$. As a consequence, every such family admits strong $\varepsilon$-nets of size at most $5000h/\varepsilon$.
item.dc:creator: D\"om\"ot\"or P\'alv\"olgyi

item.title: A Proof of Blackburn's Conjecture on Non-Overlapping Codes
item.description: arXiv:2611.28776v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A code is non-overlapping if no nonempty proper prefix of a codeword is a suffix of a codeword. Let $S_n(q)$ be the largest size of a non-overlapping code of length $n$ over an alphabet of size $q$. Levenshtein proved that $S_n(q)\le c_nq^n$, where $c_n=(1/n)\bigl((n-1)/n\bigr)^{n-1}$. The codes $I^{n-1}J$, where $I$ and $J$ partition the alphabet, attain this bound when $n$ divides $q$, and Blackburn conjectured that for every $n$ and all sufficiently large $q$, the best such code is a maximum non-overlapping code. We prove this conjecture. The proof uses generating functions for the nested partitions that describe maximal non-overlapping codes. We also show that only the codes $I^{n-1}J$ with $|I|=(n-1)q/n$ and their reversals meet Levenshtein's bound.
item.dc:creator: Yeow Meng Chee

item.title: Towards a faster parameterized algorithm for Chordal Vertex Deletion
item.description: arXiv:2611.28948v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The \textsc{Chordal Vertex Deletion} (\chvd{}) problem asks whether an input graph $G$ can be made chordal by removing at most $k$ vertices. When $k$ is taken as parameter, this problem is known to be fixed-parameter tractable \cite{M10,CM16}. However, it is still open whether \chvd{} admits a single-exponential FPT algorithm, i.e. an algorithm with running time $O(\alpha^k |V(G)|^c)$ for some constant $\alpha$ independent of $k$. Towards this goal, we describe an FPT algorithm for the compression version of \chvd{} with the following specification. Given an instance $I = (G,k,X)$ of the disjoint \chvd{} compression problem such that $|X| = k+1$, $G - X$ is chordal and its longest chordless path has length $L$, we solve $I$ in time $O((L+1)^{3k} k^2 |V(G)|^4)$.
item.dc:creator: Sylvain Guillemot

item.title: Exact edge cover by strict and non-strict temporal walks
item.description: arXiv:2611.28954v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Exact edge cover asks whether the edges of a temporal graph with $n$ vertices and $m$ edges can be partitioned into time-respecting walks with a prescribed number of walks starting at each vertex and, in the fixed-end variant, ending at each vertex. For non-strict walks, we prove that the problem is polynomially solvable by a new approach based on M-convexity, which also closes a gap in the proof sketch of an earlier static reduction. An orientation of the edges is realizable by walks exactly when walk counters stay non-negative and every snapshot component contains a walk, and only components with all degrees and counters even can violate the latter condition. Once a dead state is removed, the states of each such component form an M-convex set. This yields an augmenting path algorithm that returns walks or an infeasibility certificate, using at most $m/2$ augmentations and $O(n+nm^2)$ arithmetic operations with path-reversing re-orientation. The implementation was validated on small instances. For strict walks, we prove that the problem is NP-complete, already with six time labels for prescribed ends and two for free ends.
item.dc:creator: Duc Thien Quach, Manh Cuong Tran

item.title: On the General Position Number of Cacti
item.description: arXiv:2611.29136v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Given a graph G=(V,E), where V is the set of vertices and E is the set of edges, a subset of vertices $S \subseteq V$ is called a General Position Set (GPS) if no shortest path on G between any two vertices in S contains another vertex from S. The General Position Number (GPN) of a graph G is the maximum size of a GPS in G. The decision version of this problem, determining whether the GPN of a graph G is at least a given integer i, is known as the General Position Problem (GPP). The GPP is known to be NP-complete, making the computation of the GPN for general graphs computationally challenging. Hence, much of the existing research has focused on determining the GPN for special classes of graphs. One such class is that of cactus graphs (i.e., cacti), in which any two simple cycles share at most one vertex and no edge. For cactus graphs, several upper and lower bounds on the GPN have been previously presented. In this paper, we determine the exact value of the GPN for cactus graphs. We propose a novel graph decomposition that partitions a cactus graph into two types of subgraphs, called bearded cycles and non-beard trees. For each subgraph, we compute a special GPS, named a subGPS. We prove that the union of all maximum subGPSs constitutes a maximum GPS for the original cactus graph. This result allows us to compute the exact GPN for any cactus graph.
item.dc:creator: Toshihiko Kimura, Yonghwan Kim, Yoshiaki Katayama

item.title: An $n^{1/O(\log^* n)}$ Lower Bound for Online Coloring of $k$-Colorable Graphs
item.description: arXiv:2611.29672v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In online coloring, the vertices of a graph arrive one at a time with their edges to earlier vertices, and each vertex must be colored irrevocably on arrival. For graphs promised to be $k$-colorable, with $k\ge 3$ fixed, the best deterministic algorithms use $n^{1-\Theta(1/k^2)}$ colors, while the best lower bound was Vishwanathan's $\Omega(\log^{k-1}n)$ from 1990 until Li recently proved $2^{\Omega((\log n)^{1/3}(\log\log n)^{2/3})}$. For every fixed $k\ge 3$ and all sufficiently large $n$, we prove a lower bound of $n^{1/(\log^*n+3)}$ colors for deterministic online algorithms on $n$-vertex $k$-colorable graphs, and the same lower bound in expectation for randomized online algorithms. Both bounds hold on a single triangle-free $3$-colorable graph: even an algorithm that is shown this graph in advance, but is not told which of its vertices each arriving vertex is, can be forced to use this many colors by a suitable arrival order. The hard instances are iterated blow-ups of a clique, in which every vertex becomes a block of independent vertices and every edge a private server in the earlier block; each blow-up keeps the forced colors and replaces the chromatic number $\chi$ by about $\log\chi$, so about $\log^*n$ blow-ups bring it down to $k$. We also show that deterministic lower bounds for different values of $k\ge 3$ are polynomially equivalent, and that no adversary presenting such iterated blow-ups can force more than $n^{1/(\log^*n-O(1))}$ colors. All numbered results are formalized in Lean 4.
item.dc:creator: Sajad Faghfoor Maghrebi

item.title: Parity-safe digraphs with countably many ends are kernel-perfect
item.description: arXiv:2611.29786v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A kernel of a digraph is an independent set that every other vertex points into, and a digraph is kernel-perfect if every induced subgraph has a kernel. A digraph without odd cycles in which no ray contains infinitely many vertices that each send an infinite fan of disjoint paths to that ray is safe. The conjecture that every safe digraph is kernel-perfect was proved earlier for digraphs with finitely many ends. We prove a stronger statement for at most countably many ends. Number the vertices of a ray, and let the type of a path that ends on the ray be the parity of the sum of its length and the number of its last vertex. A fan is mixed if it has infinitely many paths of each type, and a digraph is parity-safe if it has no odd cycle and no ray containing infinitely many vertices with a mixed fan to it. Yablo's graph (omega,<) is not parity-safe. Its variant with edges only between vertices of different parity has a kernel - it is parity-safe but not safe. Our main result is that a parity-safe digraph with at most countably many ends is kernel-perfect, and the claim for safe digraphs follows since safety implies parity-safety. The digraph may have any cardinality, and nothing is assumed about the structure of the ends, but the case of uncountably many ends remains open.
item.dc:creator: Sjur Dyrkolbotn, Michal Walicki

item.title: Online Disk Hitting via Two-Point Traces
item.description: arXiv:2611.31034v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In the online hitting set problem for disks, a set $P$ of $n$ points in the plane is given in advance, and disks intersecting $P$ arrive one at a time. After each arrival, the algorithm must maintain a hitting set $X\subseteq P$ for all disks seen so far. The algorithm can only add points to $X$, and the objective is to minimize the final size of $X$. Even and Smorodinsky gave an $O(\log n)$-competitive algorithm for unit disks and asked whether the $O(\log^2 n)$ bound for disks of arbitrary radii could be improved. For arbitrary radii, our randomized algorithm selects $O(k(1+\log(n/k)))$ points in expectation on every fixed request sequence, where $k$ is the size of a minimum hitting set for that sequence. This gives an $O(\log n)$ expected competitive ratio. For every $k$, we prove a matching lower bound on the worst-case expected cost, even on collinear point sets. The algorithm samples priority orders on $P$ in advance. For each arriving disk $D$, it selects the first point of $D\cap P$ in the current order. The same expected cost bound holds for shortest-path balls in graphs excluding a fixed minor, with a matching lower bound on paths.
item.dc:creator: Mingchao Zhou, Chunying Ren, Yingli Ran, Zhao Zhang

item.title: Cop-Win Edge Completion: Hardness, Structure, and Parameterized Algorithm
item.description: arXiv:2611.31191v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study Cop-Win Edge Completion: given a graph $G$, find the minimum number $\copfill(G)$ of edges whose addition lets one cop capture a visible robber. We first give an exact reduction from Dominating Set, constructing for every nonempty graph $H$ a graph $G_H$ on $2|V(H)|+2$ vertices with $\copfill(G_H)=\gamma(H)$. This resolves a complexity question of Mertzios et al. and implies NP-completeness even for connected graphs of diameter two with a dominating edge and domination number two. Interestingly, while Minimum Fill-in is fixed-parameter tractable in the number $k$ of added edges, Cop-Win Edge Completion, whose target class strictly contains the connected chordal graphs, is W[2]-hard parameterized by $k$, even by $k+\gamma(G)$. We then give two lower bounds. The first, $\copfill(G)\ge 2n-m-b-c-1$, where $n,m,b,c$ count vertices, edges, nontrivial blocks, and components, is tight for partial 2-trees, giving a linear-time algorithm for the optimum value and a quadratic-time construction; for outerplanar graphs, an optimum completion preserving outerplanarity is found in linear time. The second, based on the cycle space modulo the subspace generated by triangles, gives $\copfill(G)=c-1+\sum_{i=1}^r(\ell_i-3)$ for block-cactus graphs with long cycle blocks of lengths $\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_r$. We also show how the optimum behaves under disjoint unions and joins, yielding a polynomial-time algorithm for $P_4$-sparse graphs, including cographs, and exact formulas for complete multipartite graphs. In contrast to partial 2-trees and block-cactus graphs, an optimum cop-win completion can be much smaller than a minimum chordal one, already on complete bipartite graphs. Finally, we give FPT algorithms for $k+\mathrm{nd}(G)$, for the twin-cover number $t$ alone in time $2^{O(t^3)}n^{O(1)}$, and for $k+\mathrm{tw}(G)$.
item.dc:creator: Rajat Adak

item.title: Approximating TSP walks in subcubic graphs
item.description: arXiv:2112.06278v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We prove that every simple 2-connected subcubic graph on $n$ vertices with $n_2$ vertices of degree 2 has a TSP walk of length at most $\frac{5n+n_2}{4}-1$, confirming a conjecture of Dvo\v{r}\'ak, Kr\'al', and Mohar. This bound is best possible; there are infinitely many subcubic and cubic graphs whose minimum TSP walks have lengths $\frac{5n+n_2}{4}-1$ and $\frac{5n}{4} - 2$ respectively. We characterize the extremal subcubic examples meeting this bound. We also give a quadratic-time combinatorial algorithm for finding such a TSP walk. In particular, we obtain a $\frac{5}{4}$-approximation algorithm for the graphic TSP on simple cubic graphs, improving on the previously best known approximation ratio of $\frac{9}{7}$.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Journal of Combinatorial Theory, Series B 158 (2023), 70-104
item.dc:creator: Michael C. Wigal, Youngho Yoo, Xingxing Yu

item.title: Oriented trees in $O(k \sqrt{k})$-chromatic digraphs, a subquadratic bound for Burr's conjecture
item.description: arXiv:2402.19351v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In 1980, Burr conjectured that every directed graph with chromatic number $2k-2$ contains any oriented tree of order $k$ as a subdigraph. Burr showed that chromatic number $(k-1)^2$ suffices, and this was later improved to $\frac{k^2}{2} - \frac{k}{2} + 1$ by Addario-Berry, Havet, Linhares-Sales, Reed and Thomass\'e. We prove the first subquadratic bound for Burr's conjecture: every digraph with chromatic number $\frac{8}{3} k \sqrt{k} + 7k$ contains any oriented tree of order $k$. Moreover, we provide improved bounds of $\sqrt{4/3} k \sqrt{k}+k/2$ for arborescences, and $\frac{(b+3)}{2}k$ for paths with $b$ blocks.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Journal of Combinatorial Theory Series B 182 (2027), 106-125
item.dc:creator: St\'ephane Bessy, Daniel Gon\c{c}alves, Amadeus Reinald

item.title: nni+: a local subtree-move distance for mutation trees
item.description: arXiv:2501.07529v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Mutation trees describe the order in which somatic mutations accumulate in a tumor. Inference from noisy sequencing data yields many plausible trees, so comparing mutation trees is a basic task, and a distance is most useful when its value has a direct evolutionary meaning. Rearrangement distances have this meaning: they count how many local corrections separate two evolutionary histories. However, the classical local move, the nearest neighbor interchange (NNI), does not suit mutation trees, where every node carries a mutation, because it preserves the number of children of every node and so cannot connect all trees. We propose nni+, which moves a set of sibling subtrees one level up or down and corresponds to stating that a mutation occurred before or after a group of subclones branched off. We compare it with its elementary version, which moves one subtree at a time, and with the rotation-free generalized NNI (gNNI), which exchanges subtrees across an edge in both directions. We show that nni+ induces a metric with diameter 2n-2, and we give a 2-approximation for nni+ and for gNNI. Our main result is that the nni+ distance has an exact formula and can be computed in polynomial time, whereas both the elementary distance and the rotation-free gNNI distance are NP-complete. The key is to view a mutation tree as a family of compatible clusters, in which every move replaces a single cluster. For the elementary distance we also characterize, by a linear-time test, when it coincides with the parent--child distance.
item.dc:creator: Lu\'is Cunha, Jack Kuipers, Thiago Lopes

item.title: Efficient space reduction techniques by optimized majority rules for the Kemeny aggregation problem
item.description: arXiv:2506.15097v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The Kemeny aggregation problem consists of computing the consensus rankings of an election with respect to the Kemeny-Young voting method. These consensus rankings satisfy various fundamental properties and are the geometric medians of the votes in the election under the Kendall tau distance, which counts the number of pairwise disagreements. The NP-hard Kemeny aggregation problem admits important applications in various domains such as operations research, computational social choice, machine learning, and biology but faces a severe bottleneck in practice. In 2020, Milosz and the second author presented an approach to reduce the search space of the problem by solving the relative order of pairs of elements in those consensus rankings. In this article, we prove an optimized and fully parallelizable extension of this approach. We achieve significantly more space reduction while the parallel design reduces the time complexity from ${O}(n^3)$ to essentially ${O}(n^2)$ with significant computational speedups in practice. We then show how the constraints built by our approach can be rigorously combined with other methods such as Integer Programming and Finest Condorcet Partitioning to achieve a highly efficient, robust, and scalable solution approach to the Kemeny aggregation problem. Our methods are applicable to the more general constrained Kemeny aggregation ranking problem with immutable input pairwise constraints. Experiments with benchmark against the commercial solver Gurobi are performed on real and synthetic data.
item.dc:creator: Xuan Kien Phung, Sylvie Hamel

item.title: Fractional domatic number and minimum degree
item.description: arXiv:2508.19617v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The domatic number of a graph $G$ is the maximum number of pairwise disjoint dominating sets of $G$. We are interested in the LP-relaxation of this parameter, which is called the fractional domatic number of $G$. We study its extremal value in the class of graphs of minimum degree $d$. The fractional domatic number of a graph of minimum degree $d$ is always at most $d+1$, and at least $(1-o(1))\, d/\ln d$ as $d\to \infty$. This is asymptotically tight even within the class of split graphs. Our main result concerns the case $d=2$; we show that, excluding $8$ exceptional graphs, the fractional domatic number of every connected graph of minimum degree (at least) $2$ is at least $5/2$. We also show that this bound cannot be improved if only finitely many graphs are excluded, even for bipartite graphs of arbitrarily large girth. This proves in a stronger sense a conjecture by Gadouleau, Harms, Mertzios, and Zamaraev (2024). This also extends and generalises results from McCuaig and Shepherd (1989), from Fujita, Kameda, and Yamashita (2000), and from Abbas, Egerstedt, Liu, Thomas, and Whalen (2016). Finally, we show that graphs of sub-exponential expansion and sufficiently large girth $g$ have fractional domatic number $3 - o_g(1)$.
item.dc:creator: Quentin Chuet, Hugo Demaret, Hoang La, Fran\c{c}ois Pirot

item.title: Minimally tough series-parallel graphs with toughness at least $1/2$
item.description: arXiv:2512.01905v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Let $t$ be a positive real number. A graph is called \emph{$t$-tough} if the removal of any vertex set $S$ that disconnects the graph leaves at most $|S|/t$ components. The toughness of a graph is the largest $t$ for which the graph is $t$-tough. A graph is minimally $t$-tough if the toughness of the graph is $t$, and the deletion of any edge from the graph decreases the toughness. Series--parallel graphs are graphs with two distinguished vertices called terminals, formed recursively by two simple composition operations, series and parallel joins. They can be used to model series and parallel electric circuits. We characterize minimally $t$-tough series--parallel graphs for all $t\ge 1/2$. It is clear that there is no minimally $t$-tough series--parallel graph if $t>1$. We show that, for $1\ge t >1/2$, most of the series--parallel graphs with toughness $t$ are minimally $t$-tough, but most of the series--parallel graphs with toughness $1/2$ are not minimally $1/2$-tough.
item.dc:creator: Gyula Y. Katona, Humara Khan

item.title: Structural Classes for Chollet's Permanent Conjecture
item.description: arXiv:2604.24192v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In 1982, Chollet conjectured that $\operatorname{per}(A\circ B)\le \operatorname{per}(A)\operatorname{per}(B)$ for Hermitian positive semidefinite matrices $A,B$, where $\circ$ denotes the Hadamard (entrywise) product. In this paper, we study natural structural classes for which the conjecture holds. We first show that a stronger inequality holds for a broad class of matrices with bipartite support. We then introduce a simple way of joining positive semidefinite matrices and give conditions under which Chollet's inequality is preserved under this operation. For graph Laplacians, this operation corresponds to vertex coalescence and gives larger structured graph families satisfying Chollet's inequality from simpler graph classes.
item.dc:creator: Priyanshu Pant, Ranveer Singh

item.title: Boolean threshold functions, neuron capacity, and memory retrieval
item.description: arXiv:2609.29756v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: How much information can a single neuron remember? How many memories can neural networks retrieve without creating false memories? These questions are related to a basic question: how many Boolean threshold functions $f(x)=\operatorname{sgn}(a_0+\langle a,x\rangle)$, $x\in\{-1,1\}^n$, are there? In this paper, we show that the number $T_n$ of distinct Boolean threshold functions is \[ T_n=2\binom{2^n-1}{n}\bigl(1+O(n^{-99})\bigr). \] Equivalently, the capacity of a single threshold neuron is $n^2-\log_2(n!)+1+O(n^{-99})$ bits, improving the $O(n)$ error term in the result of Kahn--Koml\'os--Szemer\'edi to $O(n^{-99})$. To prove this, we show that, for $1\le r\le n-1$, and $v_1,\ldots,v_r$ are chosen at random from $\{-1,1\}^n$, \[ \mathbb P\!\left\{ \langle v_1,\ldots,v_r\rangle\cap\{-1,1\}^n =\{\pm v_1,\ldots,\pm v_r\} \right\} =1-O(n^{-99}). \] In the context of the Kanter--Sompolinsky Hamiltonian for memory retrieval, this identifies $r=n-1$ as a sharp threshold, at which, for almost every collection of $r$ memories, the only ground states are these memories and their negatives, confirming a weaker form of the Kalai--Linial--Odlyzko conjecture. It also settles a recent open problem posed by M. Anthony on the specification number of Boolean threshold functions. In addition, we show that, for every $1\le r\le n-1$, \[ \mathbb P\{v_1,\ldots,v_r\text{ are linearly dependent}\} =2\binom r2\,2^{-n}+O\!\left(2^{-n}e^{-cn}\right), \] confirming a conjecture of Kahn--Koml\'os--Szemer\'edi.
item.dc:creator: Xinyuan Xie

item.title: Avoiding Distances
item.description: arXiv:2610.24803v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Given a finite planar point set $X=\{x_1,\ldots,x_n\}$, let $a_1<a_2< \cdots < a_s$ denote the $s \leq {n \choose 2}$ different (Euclidean) distances between points in $X$. The aim is to retain as many of the points as possible such that certain imposed inter-pair distances are avoided. For example, we show that: (A) Given a set $X$ of $n$ points in the plane, an independent set of size $0.2293 n$ in the unit distance graph determined by $X$ can be found in $O(n^2)$ time. For any fixed $k \in \mathbf{N}$ there exists a constant $c_k>0$ such that for any set $X$ of $n$ points in the plane, and set $D$ of size $k$, there exists a subset $X' \subseteq X$ of size $|X'| \geq c_k |X|$ in which no pair of points is at some distance in $D$ (we say that $X'$ avoids distances in $D$). Such a set can be found efficiently. (B) (i) There is a subset of $X$ of size $n/2$ that avoids the maximum distance; this bound cannot be improved. (ii) There is a subset of $X$ of size $8n/47$ that avoids both the minimum and maximum distance; on the other hand, there exists $X$ such that at most $5n/16$ points can be retained with this property. (iii) There is a subset of $X$ of size $n/7$ whose diameter is at most half the original diameter; on the other hand, there exists $X$ such that at most $n/6$ points can be retained with this property. (C) (i) For any $\varepsilon>0$, a $(1-\varepsilon)$-approximation for \textsc{MIS} in the minimum distance graph of $n$ points in the plane can be found in $2^{O(1/\varepsilon)} n^{O(1)}$ time. (ii) Given a set $X$ of $n$ points in the plane, a maximum independent set in the graph of diameters can be computed in $O(n \log{n})$ time. The techniques used to handle the planar case can be extended to $\mathbf{R}^d$ for any fixed dimension $d$.
item.dc:creator: Adrian Dumitrescu, Zsolt L\'angi
